findings.title: A pool whose hook address has no code on its own network freezes every position when the address sets a removal flag, and live pools on Polygon and Avalanche hold third-party positions frozen this way
findings.difference: No opcode difference: on all 21 networks a call to an address without code returns success and no data (measured). The networks differ only in which hook addresses are empty: the hook 0xf8c3f4243c4d8c02831a718a7978fd869f094300 (bits 9 and 8) has 2,488 bytes of code on Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain and Arbitrum One and none on Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, World Chain and Avalanche, because it was deployed through the CREATE2 deployer 0x4e59b44847b379578588920ca78fbf26c0b4956c on some networks only, and pool creators on the others named the same address.
findings.mechanism: 1. initialize checks only the low 14 bits of the hook address and never reads its code (src/PoolManager.sol:126, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). 2. For liquidityDelta <= 0, beforeModifyLiquidity calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204) and afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:232-243); donate calls the donate hooks for bits 5 and 4 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:317-335). 3. callHook makes a plain CALL with all gas (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). An address without code returns success and no data, so result.length < 32 and the call reverts with InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). The only bypass is msg.sender == hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217), which nobody holds for an empty address. 4. This cycle measured the call on all 21 networks: an eth_call from each PoolManager address with beforeRemoveLiquidity calldata to three seeded random addresses, to 0x...20, to 0x...dead0030 and to every empty hook address of that network returned success with empty data in all 199 calls (raw/emptycall.json), so the freeze has the same shape everywhere. 5. findings.impact: Principal and fees of every position in such a pool, for every holder. Measured third-party exposure is dust: on Polygon about 0.019 POL and 0.0015 USDC across two positions, on Avalanche about 0.045 AVAX and 0.32 USDt across six positions, plus whatever BNB Smart Chain and Base add (see mechanism). No funds outside these pools are reachable, because the deltas of a removal only involve the pool's own currencies and its hook.
findings.preconditions: A pool creator names a flagged address that has no code on that network, and other accounts add liquidity. No role is needed for either step. The third-party owners in the Polygon and Avalanche pools are smart accounts and EOAs that also create pools on the same hooks, so they may be one operator; that link was not established.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and routers should read the code at the hook address on the network itself before listing a pool or adding liquidity, and should not infer it from another network. Core could reject an empty hook address in initialize, which would not stop later loss of code (F-013).
